title: Screen Time May Matter Most at Ages 1 and 6, Scientists Find
summary:
When you watch a screen may matter just as much as how long you watch. A study that followed children from age 1 to 8 found extra screen time at ages 1 and 6 was linked to weaker school results at age 9 and weaker working memory at age 10 and a half. Working memory is the brain's ability to hold and juggle information — following instructions, solving math problems, and keeping track of ideas.

Scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore studied 502 children in Singapore, tracking them in the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes birth cohort. Parents reported screen habits at six points from infancy to middle childhood, and researchers tested school achievement and working memory years later. The study was published in the World Journal of Pediatrics.

The link was strongest at age 1. "The effect sizes we saw at age 1 were the largest among all time points we examined," the authors said, adding that early infancy may be a window when the developing brain is especially sensitive to screens replacing learning interactions. Screen use at ages 2 and 3 showed no clear link, but it reappeared at age 6, when children start formal schooling.

Screens may crowd out brain-building activities like talking with caregivers, imaginative play, and hands-on exploring. The study shows only a link, not proof that screens directly cause weaker results. Still, the researchers say less is better: an extra hour of daily screen time may not change one child's results much, but across a whole population, small dips could mean more children struggling in school. The World Health Organization and the American Academy of Pediatrics advise no screens in the first 18 to 24 months and under one hour a day for ages 2 to 5.
why_it_matters: Small dips in learning across a whole population could mean more children struggling in school, so knowing which ages matter most helps families and health groups give better advice on screen time.

background_read: A child's brain grows very fast in the first years of life, and what a child does each day helps shape how it develops.
Talking with adults, playing, and exploring hands-on give the brain practice in paying attention, remembering things, and solving problems.
Scientists study groups of children over many years to see how early habits connect with later learning, by asking parents about daily life and testing children's skills as they grow older.
Health groups give advice on screen time because they want to help families balance screens with the activities that build a young brain.
